https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/141101.text: Hungary shuts sole nuclear plant due to drought, PM flags 'Critical' days ahead Authorities are preparing to halt operations at the Paks nuclear plant as falling Danube River water levels threaten cooling capacity Hungary has completely powered down the Paks Nuclear Power Plant—its only nuclear facility for the first time in its 44-year history. The descion came after the country faces a critical challenge looming ahead. as large parts of Europe have been hit by prolonged heat and drought, lowering river levels and raising concerns about water supplies, river transport and power generation. Notably, severe drought across Central Europe has caused the Danube River (used to cool the reactors) to plunge to record-low water levels. The plant normally provides roughly a third to 40% of Hungary's electricity. Prime Minister Peter Magyar warned of a looming energy crisis, prompting emergency power imports, restrictions on heavy industrial energy/water consumption, and public appeals for power conservation. New challenges: Hungary's 2 gigawatt Paks power plant, which runs four Russian-built reactors, was operating at just over 10% of its total capacity on Sunday after the Danube, whose waters it uses as a coolant, fell to a record low. The water authority was projecting that the level of the river, which flows from Germany to the Black Sea, would drop further in the coming days. "We are facing the most critical five days ahead," Magyar said in a Facebook video. "Tomorrow, the Paks power plant will ‌not be generating, while the hottest, 40-degree (Celsius, 104 Fahrenheit) days are ahead. "The power grid, our public services and ourselves will all come under enormous strain," said Magyar, who has warned that Paks could remain idle for weeks. According to government records, Falls in water levels have also disrupted shipping ​and tourism in Hungary ​and triggered water-use restrictions ⁠in more than 100 cities and villages, including on the outskirts of Budapest. Magyar reiterated a call for ​companies, public institutions, local governments and households to significantly reduce ​or reschedule ⁠electricity use during evening peak hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m. The ​crisis could cost Hungary 100 billion to 200 billion ​forints ($315 million to $630 million) due to the surging price of imported electricity, Mark Radnai, vice chairman of ​Magyar's Tisza party, said on Facebook. The PM said government will decide on Sunday whether to apply mandatory electricity use restrictions for large companies from Monday. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp8e.text: Image source, Joe Giddens/PA Wire Image caption, Jahvine Kwamba admitted two counts of misconduct in judicial or public office, and a charge of transmitting an image and sound from prison without authority in March Published 7 August 2026 A prison officer who sent sexually explicit photos on Snapchat to a drug dealer who styled himself as the "Latvian Pablo Escobar" has been jailed for eight months. Jahvine Kwamba, 21, was working at HMP Fosse Way in Leicestershire when she began a relationship with prisoner Roberts Sokolovs in 2024, Leicester Crown Court heard. Kwamba, of Old Hall Crescent, Bentley, Doncaster, pleaded guilty in March to two counts of misconduct in judicial or public office, and a charge of transmitting an image and sound from prison without authority. Sentencing Kwamba on Friday, Judge Timothy Spencer KC said he suspected Kwamba was "pretty lonely and vulnerable", adding "you were easy prey" for Sokolovs. Sokolovs was imprisoned for drug-related matters in 2022 due to his involvement in a County Lines drug ring called the Jimmy Line, between Skelmersdale in Lancashire and Lincoln. Prosecutor Rawaid Javed said sexually explicit photographs and messages were sent between the pair on Snapchat after Sokolovs was sent to an immigration removal centre at Gatwick Airport in June 2024. The court was told because he was deported to Latvia in November that year, Sokolovs was never interviewed about his relationship with Kwamba. While at HMP Fosse Way, there were 5,441 contacts with each other on Snapchat, and 4,211 contacts between them while Sokolovs was at the removal centre. Kwamba denies there was any physical sexual contact between the pair, which the prosecutor said he was "sceptical" about. The 21-year-old also received five payments from Sokolovs's mother Zita Sokolova, 53, totalling Â£1,495 between 18 March and 2 July 2024, while 18 payments totalling Â£4,665 were sent to her in the same period by his 20-year-old sister Venera Sokolova. Kwamba sent seven payments, totalling Â£660, to his sister between 27 March and 1 July 2024. Image source, PA Media Image caption, Kwamba, 21, was working at HMP Fosse Way in Leicestershire when she began a relationship with prisoner Roberts Sokolovs Javed said there were "no obvious patterns" to the transactions, and when Kwamba first received a payment of Â£500 from Zita Sokolova in March 2024, she spent it on food and clothing and did not transfer it. Sam Ponniah, defending Kwamba, who was 19 at the time of the offences, said she had shown "significant levels of naivety and immaturity". He added she had been "well in over her head" when she was put in charge of 64 prisoners despite being a prison officer for about four months. "She speaks about the fact when she first got this job, being away from home, she was in an area she was unfamiliar with and living by herself," Ponniah added. 'Struck at the heart' Venera Sokolova was in contact with her brother while he was in prison 191 times, while his mother Zita Sokolova was in contact with him 33 times. Venera and Zita, both from Alderley, Skelmersdale, Lancashire, previously pleaded guilty to transmitting or causing the transmission of an image by electronic communications from inside HMP Fosse Way between 24 February and 3 June 2024. Zita Sokolova was given a four-month prison sentence, suspended for one year, and ordered to pay Â£400 costs. Venera Sokolova was given a 12-month community order with a requirement to attend 15 probation appointments. Judge Timothy Spencer KC said: "This case strikes at the heart of any functioning criminal justice system, including a functioning prison system, where those running a prison can have some confidence that discipline and good order is maintained and not continually undermined. "You, in your different ways, have all contributed to the undermining of that system of law and order and each of you have struck at the heart of the maintenance of law and order in this country." https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Hundreds of thousands of protestors in France have gathered to demonstrate against what they call an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system. Photograph: Véronique de Viguerie/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Hundreds of thousands of protestors in France have gathered to demonstrate against what they call an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system. Photograph: Véronique de Viguerie/Getty Images First Edition newsletter France Thursday briefing: Why young people are taking to the streets across France In today’s newsletter: A youth-led movement is protesting crumbling school buildings and teacher shortages while turning adult focus onto wider educational inequalities Libby Brooks Thu 8 Oct 2026 01.43 EDT Last modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 01.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. In my experience, at any protest, the most memorable and encapsulating slogans are always the ones written by hand with marker pen on cardboard placards. “School is a right, not a privilege,” read one such sign held aloft by a student in Paris , where huge youth protests over the state of high school education have brought tens of thousands of young people and adults on to the streets, with further strikes planned today. “A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” another sign said, referencing growing public anger at alleged police brutality towards young protesters. Tens of thousands of young people have also taken to Spanish streets in recent weeks to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. And outside the Labour conference in Liverpool last week, a crowd of jobless young people protested against what they saw as their bleak employment prospects. From Paris to the north of England, a similar thread runs through it all: a generation who feel betrayed by the absence of basic economic security and the erosion of public services that older generations took for granted. I spoke to our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis who has been reporting from the centre of the French protests. But first, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich. Education | Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found. Spain | María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died. Science | A type of gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science is safe and can partly restore sight in blind people , researchers have revealed. Epstein | British billionaire Sir James Goldsmith warned that Jeffrey Epstein was a “sexual deviant” decades before the FBI closed in on the abuser, a Guardian investigation has found. In depth: Why have young people taken to the streets? View image in fullscreen ‘School is a right, not a privilege’ … students take to the streets in Paris. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters The most significant youth movement to emerge across France in recent decades started on 17 September. Pupils returning to the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, southwest of Paris, after the summer holidays, discovered they couldn’t continue their studies because of the extent of staff absences. The 15- to 18-year-olds blockaded their high school in protest. After negotiations with the education ministry, those staffing gaps were filled, but the impassioned complaints about crumbling buildings, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days – alongside a wider sense of inequality in the education system – resonated in the suburbs. “This movement grew from the ground up, from teenagers speaking to others outside their lycées . And over a couple of weeks, it has spread to hundreds of schools across France,” Angelique tells me. There’s a tendency to mythologise youth protest, especially in France – my uncle Joss was in Paris in 1968, and I lapped up his tales of pulling up cobblestones with his bare hands to build barricades. But youth activism is often diminished. When I reported on the schoolchildren who protested against the war in Iraq in 2003 , and those who took part in climate strikes more than a decade later, adults repeatedly questioned whether they were swayed by older provocateurs or just wanted an excuse to dodge school and indulge in petty vandalism. (In my experience: no, no and no.) So it is in France this past month. “This is very much a youth movement,” says Angelique, comparing it to similar protests in 2006 over an unpopular youth employment contract, which were organised by students’ unions. “High schoolers are organising themselves without a centralised system or even spokesperson. That’s historic, and it’s taken the government by surprise.” Who are the teenagers on the streets? This week, the sociologist Fabien Truong, who has written widely on youth protest culture, praised the “maturity and coherence” of the protesters. He pointed to a “social media effect” whereby teenagers in wealthier areas were sharing videos of scurrying rats, gaping ceilings and leaking toilets in poorer schools. “It’s beautiful, this solidarity with students from more privileged backgrounds fighting for others and more equality.” This is precisely what Angelique has witnessed on the streets of Paris in recent days, where some of the most elite state schools have also been barricaded. She spoke to one teacher outside a school in a richer inner-city area, who was proud of her pupils. “She said there was a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers, and how it flies in the face of the idea that they’re part of a social media generation who are selfish and narcissistic.” “I spent a long time speaking to teenage girls at one of the barricades in the centre of the city,” Angelique says,“who were sitting on top of a pile of bins and shopping trolleys. They told me: ‘We’re told in France that state education is a great leveller, but that’s not the case. We are being taught our lessons, but we’re getting out on to the street because we can’t bear to know that other students in poorer areas are in buildings that are crumbling’.” *** What’s wrong with French schools? As Angelique sets out in this helpful explainer , the pupils’ grievances are backed up by evidence – and the prime minister himself has described them as “legitimate”. Thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, are in need of repair. Class sizes are bigger on average, and school days are longer, than in other comparable countries, while about 10% of teaching hours across the year are not delivered because of absent teachers. And yet France’s expenditure on high schools is 28% higher than the OECD average. What’s going on? The high spend can be explained in various ways, Angelique tells me. France has a lot more high school buildings to maintain than other countries, and many more vocational courses that cost more to teach. At the same time, more spending is desperately needed on staff. Teacher shortages are linked to very low pay progression through the profession, while there are severe difficulties in finding teachers to work in deprived areas. There’s also a shortfall in other crucial roles, including school nurses and support staff for pupils with disabilities. How have adults responded ? Angelique tells me that what has defined how adults are responding to this burgeoning movement is the behaviour of politicians and police. Initially, the French government “had its head in the sand”, she says, distracted by public anger at rising fuel costs and a difficult budget process. “And when it suddenly woke up, the reaction was not a political one, it was a police crackdown.” Eighteen investigations into possible police brutality are already under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after contact with a stun grenade and a 14-year-old whose jaw was shattered after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. Yesterday, the French interior minister suspended the use of stun grenades but rejected accusations of police brutality, saying riot officers only intervened when protesters turned violent. Dozens of teachers have also been injured in clashes, and a small number of schools burned or ransacked, but Angelique tells me that most protests have been peaceful. The injuries, however, have prompted outrage, with parents and teachers angry at the “disproportionate police response” now joining young people at the barricades. An Elabe poll for BFMTV, published on Wednesday, found that 72% of French people thought the student’s demands were legitimate – although 55% of of those surveyed also thought the protests should come to an end. The movement has also brought to the fore a debate about the wider state of public services ahead of next year’s presidential election. The radical left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, backed for president by 47% of voters under 35 , is loudly supporting the protesters, while far-right candidate Marine Le Pen has blamed the current government for chaos and called for an anti-riot law. The sheer scale of the marches in cities across France this week was unexpected, Angelique says. “There were hundreds of thousands of parents, grandparents and teachers. There is a lot of support for these young people’s demands and an understanding that the problems they are raising reflect wider worries about public services.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen ‘Our bodies must be in continuous contact!’ Daphne and Niles in the actors’ favourite scene. The Latest Photograph: The Guardian Christa Pike awake and speaking after botched execution: what happens now? Christa Pike, a death row inmate who survived the state of Tennessee’s attempt to execute her last week, is conscious and speaking. The 50-year-old is recovering in hospital after surviving two lethal injections in a case that has shocked many in the US and prompted a debate about the death penalty. She was due to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Michael Safi speaks to the chief reporter for Guardian US, Ed Pilkington . Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron View image in fullscreen Illustration: Ella Baron/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Luis Gómez, known as JM, sings with Los Cracks del Puerto at the SCD Hall in Santiago, Chile. Photograph: Tamara Merino/The Guardian At 65 years old, Luis Gómez was still hawking vegetables at the market he had worked at since the age of eight. Now at 80, Gomes, or JM as he is popularly known, has become a musical sensation , selling out venues across Chile, as well as in Mexico, the UK, Argentina and France. He is the frontman of Los Crack del Puerto, who in May released their fourth record, Lo Mucho Que Nos Queda (So Much Yet to Come), as a cassette – to great acclaim. It’s a long way from his early life in the city of Valparaíso; the youngest of five children, he was three when his father died, and 10 when he lost his mother. For a time, he slept on the street between parked cars. JM would eventually form a musical double act with his cousin, Juan Navarro, and the two entertained crowds in Valparaíso’s bars. The pair would find fame well into their 70s after forming the band in 2017. “I never planned any of this, and I’d be happy still working at the market,” JM says. “But I suppose it’s never too late to give something a try.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work?
